packs.title: Parks and City Life
packs.promise: Explore central museums, Cholon street heritage and separate river and lake outings.

q.s: Collect an object’s visible evidence and its stated history.
st: Enter with a valid museum ticket and find the Peace Bell using the visitor information or staff directions.
Look at the bell’s surface, its suspended striker and the explanatory panel without touching or operating them.
Afterwards, collect three kinds of evidence: a visible material detail, a detail of how the object works, and one fact the panel supplies about its previous use.
Write a short distinction between something you saw yourself and something you learned from the panel.

q.s: Collect the difference between a visitor path and a home.
st: Use the open ground-level alley approach from Tran Hung Dao and pause out of residents’ way.
Collect an observation about the shared circulation space, one about the upper railings seen from below, and one about a doorway or boundary that separates a home from the path.
For each, write what you can see and what it tells you about moving through this residential place. Do not identify residents or document private possessions.
Make a short visitor rule of your own based on those observations, such as keeping a doorway clear.

q.s: Create a composition that changes with the bridge’s perspective.
st: From an open public approach, look at the real curve of the bridge and how it meets the lake-side ground.
Choose a second nearby public-path viewpoint that changes the overlap of deck, rail and background, without leaving the ordinary visitor area.
Create a two-view drawing or two written composition descriptions. Keep the same bridge feature in both and explain what changed with your position.
Give your work an original short title, without inventing a lighting show or entering a private terrace.

packs.title: Two City Walks
packs.promise: Explore maps, architecture, books, art and the river in one connected downtown area.

q.s: Turn a real Palace façade rhythm into an original design.
st: Enter with a Palace ticket through an operating visitor gate and view the actual façade from an admitted ground-level path.
Notice the vertical screen and a repeated spacing or opening. Remember one detail of its rhythm without making a staged photograph or drawing inside.
After you have exited and found a suitable place outside, create your own shade-screen design for a small window. Use the observed rhythm as a starting point, changing the layout to make it yours.
Annotate your sketch, or write a design proposal, explaining which observation inspired it and which feature you invented.

q.s: Collect a territory and a communications network.
st: Enter the ordinary open public hall and find the historic wall maps without interrupting postal customers.
Compare the map of Saigon and its environs, dated 1892, with the 1936 telegraph-network map of southern Vietnam and Cambodia.
Collect a visible clue to territory from the first and a visible clue to a connection from the second. You need not translate all the French labels.
After stepping aside or leaving the hall, write a different question each map helps a viewer ask. Do not treat either historic map as a present-day boundary or live route guide.

q.s: Move down Nguyen Hue and notice how the view opens.
st: Start on the ordinary public pedestrian portion near Le Loi and choose a stationary viewpoint looking riverward.
Walk along the open walking-street space toward the river, stopping before each road crossing to use the available pedestrian route.
At a second stationary point near the riverward end, notice how one visible building or the width of the view has changed.
Write a short start-and-finish comparison, then stop before crossing Ton Duc Thang for the next park mission.
